topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Make the same public object respond differently as its current mode changes. Worked example: A session with three permitted transitions. Each state returns a proposed next state. Session owns the current state and commits the replacement after the call completes. Returning no pointer is an ordinary rejected event.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Map permitted events to explicit state transitions.
Separate rejected events from accepted transitions.
Replace a state only after its current handler has returned.

blocks.text: A context holds one current state object and delegates state-dependent work through a shared State interface. Concrete states supply the behavior for their modes and participate in choosing permitted next states. Replacing the current state changes later responses while the context itself keeps its identity. The pattern organizes a state machine; an enum and switch can still be the better implementation for a small, stable machine.

cards.question: What problem does State address?
cards.answer: Make the same public object respond differently as its current mode changes. Worked example: A session with three permitted transitions. Each state returns a proposed next state. Session owns the current state and commits the replacement after the call completes. Returning no pointer is an ordinary rejected event.

cards.question: What is State?
cards.answer: A current mode whose rules affect an object behavior.

cards.question: What is Transition?
cards.answer: A permitted change from one state to another in response to an event.

cards.question: What is Context?
cards.answer: The object that owns current state and delegates state-dependent work.

cards.question: What is Transition proposal?
cards.answer: A next-state value prepared before the context commits a change.

cards.question: If the current object stays a Session, how does its behavior change?
cards.answer: Session delegates the decision to the state object it currently owns. A different concrete state handles the next call through the same interface.

cards.question: Why does next return nullptr for an invalid event?
cards.answer: The example defines that value as rejection. Session checks it and keeps the old state; it does not install a null current state.

cards.question: Why does next return a proposed state rather than delete the current state itself?
cards.answer: The current virtual call must finish before its object is destroyed. Session receives the proposal and only then replaces its owning pointer.

cards.question: What distinguishes an invalid event from a self-transition here?
cards.answer: An invalid event returns no proposal and send returns false. The context remains unchanged without constructing a replacement object.

cards.question: Could an enum and switch be simpler for three states?
cards.answer: Yes. This hierarchy demonstrates delegating behavior to state objects. For a small stable transition table, an enum can be clearer and require fewer allocations.

cards.question: Why does the capstone's enum not automatically make it the State pattern?
cards.answer: A state machine describes permitted transitions. The object-oriented State pattern specifically delegates state-dependent behavior to state objects; the capstone uses explicit guards instead.

cards.question: What test distinguishes cancel from finish?
cards.answer: Begin, then cancel, and assert idle; begin, then finish, and assert done. Both stop active work but permit different next events.

cards.question: Why keep state_ private to Session?
cards.answer: The context must control replacement timing and preserve its nonnull current state. Exposing the owner lets callers bypass transition rules or clear it.

cards.question: What should happen if allocation of a proposed state fails?
cards.answer: The exception propagates before replacement, leaving the current owned state intact. The caller can report failure without claiming the transition completed.

topics.title: The problem: one session, different rules at different times
topics.summary: A local data-import session begins idle. A begin event makes it active. A finish event is accepted only while active and moves it to done. A reset event is accepted only while done and returns it to idle. Every other event is rejected without changing the session. These rules form a finite-state machine: a system with a limited set of named states and permitted changes between them. A state is the current mode; a transition is an allowed change of mode in response to an event.

blocks.text: The simplest implementation uses an enum for the current mode and a switch for each event. That is a good choice for this three-state machine if behavior stays small. The difficulty appears when each state gains different begin, finish, status, timeout, and cleanup behavior, and those decisions spread across many switches. A maintainer can update one switch but forget another. Grouping behavior by state becomes useful when the behavior that belongs together is easier to review in one place. The object-based solution here shows that growth path without claiming it is the shortest solution to three transitions.

discussion.answer: The session starts idle, so there is no active work to finish. An event is permitted according to the current state; the event name alone does not justify a transition.

topics.title: A state object supplies behavior for the current mode
topics.summary: State declares two operations: name and next. name describes the current mode. next receives an Event and returns either an owned proposed next state or no state for rejection. Idle, Active, and Done each implement this interface. Each class therefore gathers the rules for events received while that state is current. The Session context owns exactly one State through unique_ptr and delegates event decisions to it.

blocks.text: enum class Event creates named event values whose type stays distinct from ordinary integers. Event::begin uses the scope operator to select one name from that enum. A unique_ptr<State> return value expresses exclusive ownership of a proposed state. Returning nullptr means no proposed object and therefore no accepted transition. This is a contract chosen for this example. Another design could return an explicit result with accepted, rejected, or accepted-without-change cases when internal actions need to succeed without leaving a state.

topics.title: Understand the two times when choices are made
topics.summary: The compiler checks that each concrete state supplies compatible name and next overrides. The class declarations can announce functions before their complete definitions appear. Definitions such as Active::next use the scope operator to identify the class whose member is being defined. Defining the transition functions after all three classes are complete lets make_unique construct their destination types. Forward declarations alone would not provide enough information to allocate a complete object.

blocks.text: During execution, state_->next uses virtual dispatch to call the current object’s implementation. If that object is Active, the event is compared with Event::finish. A match constructs Done; a different event returns no object. make_unique creates the destination and returns its owning pointer. The proposed pointer remains local to send until the operation decides whether to commit. If allocation throws, the old state still exists and Session has not changed its pointer. That failure differs from a rejected event, which returns false normally.

topics.title: Do not destroy the state while its method is still running
topics.summary: A dangerous implementation lets a state call a context setter that immediately deletes the current state. That setter may delete the very object whose member function is still executing. Some carefully restricted cases can avoid further access, but it is a fragile rule to maintain: adding a log that reads a member afterward can use a dead object. This design avoids the entire hazard. next only returns a proposal. Session waits for the virtual call to finish and then replaces state_.

blocks.text: The assignment state_ = std::move(proposed) transfers ownership of the new state into Session and destroys the previously owned state. std::move does not itself move bytes or call a transition; it enables the unique pointer’s move assignment. The old handler has already returned at this point. If there is no proposal, send returns false without changing state_. Session deletes copying and assignment and provides no move operation, keeping the non-null state invariant straightforward. A movable Session would need a documented rule for its moved-from state or a safe reinitialization strategy.

topics.title: Rejected events are part of the model
topics.summary: There are three states and three event values, so the primary behavior table has nine state-event combinations. Only three are accepted. The other six are not omissions; they are defined rejections. main checks all nine combinations while moving through the normal cycle. In idle, finish and reset are false. In active, begin and reset are false. In done, begin and finish are false. Each accepted event is followed by a state-name check, so a return value alone cannot hide a wrong destination.

blocks.text: This model does not perform a real import, start a thread, or wait for a file. It isolates transition logic for study. A real asynchronous import needs a rule for who sends finish and how a late completion is handled after cancellation. A generation identifier can distinguish a completion from the current run and one from an old run. Adding that protection requires a concrete asynchronous requirement; it should not be implied by a state diagram that only contains begin and finish arrows.

topics.title: State and Strategy solve different change problems
topics.summary: A strategy is a selected way to perform a task, such as choosing a sorting or compression rule. It is normally selected because a caller wants a different algorithm. State represents a mode governed by the object’s history and permitted events. Their class shapes can look alike because both delegate through an interface. Their contracts differ: selecting any next strategy may be acceptable, while jumping from idle to done without begin and finish would violate this session’s protocol.

blocks.text: For a tiny stable machine, a transition table or switch remains easier to scan than several classes and heap allocations. Choose State when state-specific behavior grows enough to justify grouping it, or when ownership of mode-specific data becomes important. The lab adds cancel only from active to idle. The key work is not adding one enum word; it is preserving the existing transitions, rejecting cancel from idle and done, and documenting what cancellation means. Testing the full expanded table reveals accidental new transitions that a single happy-path test would miss.

workshop.title: A session with three permitted transitions
workshop.problem: A session with three permitted transitions. Start idle; accept begin only from idle. Accept finish only from active and reset only from done. Reject other state/event pairs without mutation. Replace old state objects only after their handlers return.

steps.why: Only begin is permitted in Idle.
Idle returns an owned Active proposal.
Active returns Done after recognizing finish.

steps.state: Old state destroyed only during assignment in send.
steps.why: Its next member function has already returned.

workshop.pitfall: Destroy the current state inside its still-running next method. A later member access in that method can access a destroyed object. Replacing ownership can end the lifetime of the object whose method is active.

discussion.question: For a fixed vending controller with four modes and one event function, choose classes or a table and explain your preference.
discussion.answer: A table or switch is likely clearer when transitions dominate and per-state behavior is tiny. State classes become useful when each mode owns meaningful behavior or resources. Either choice must cover all state/event pairs.
discussion.hint: Count state-specific behavior, not only states.

workshop.alternative: An enum and switch are likely simpler for this exact three-state example. A table works especially well when transitions are data and behavior is small. State objects earn their cost when several state-specific operations or resources would otherwise be scattered.
workshop.design: Each state returns a proposed next state. Session owns the current state and commits the replacement after the call completes. Returning no pointer is an ordinary rejected event.
invariants: Session owns exactly one live state during public calls.
Rejected events preserve the current state.
A state handler cannot destroy its own receiver through Session.
workshop.maintenance: A new state or event changes a behavior table, not only a class list. Review permitted transitions, state-owned resources, failure behavior, and late events together.
workshop.verification: The program checks all nine primary state/event combinations, normal destination names, rejection cases, and return to idle. It does not force allocation failure or exercise asynchronous import work. The ownership sequence nevertheless leaves the old state unchanged until a proposal exists.
